AI Factory Case Studies · Part 5 · Meta Prometheus & Hyperion

Prometheus and Hyperion: How Meta Went From Tents to a 5-Gigawatt City

Meta took the fastest route it could find to a gigawatt. Prometheus in Ohio links traditional data centers, AI-designed buildings, quick-build structures and leased space into one training cluster. Hyperion in Louisiana is the opposite: one campus planned to reach 5 GW, owned mostly by investors and powered by up to ten new gas plants. This case study follows both, and shows how Meta combined the bets of the first four parts.

3. The bet: use every kind of building at once

In July 2025 Mark Zuckerberg said Meta would spend hundreds of billions of dollars on compute and named its first multi-gigawatt clusters: Prometheus, due online in 2026, and Hyperion, able to scale to 5 GW. The problem was time. A purpose-built AI data center takes years; Meta wanted a gigawatt in about a year. So for Prometheus it stopped insisting on one kind of building and used whatever could hold GPUs soonest, including quick-build structures that press reports in 2025 described as tents ⚠️, and capacity leased from partners.

💡 A hybrid of the first four betsPrometheus borrows Colossus's speed and own-generation power, and Fairwater's idea of linking buildings into one cluster. Hyperion borrows Abilene's investor-owned buildings, with Meta itself as the tenant. Meta is the first company in this series to run several bets at the same time.

5. One cluster across many sites

According to coverage of Meta's post, Prometheus links buildings from 2 km to more than 100 km apart into one training cluster of hundreds of thousands of GPUs, using GB200 and GB300 NVL72 racks, with Vera Rubin NVL72 next. Keeping a job that size running is as hard as building it. The post reports that interruptions fell by 99% ⚠️; one report puts the mid-2025 baseline at nearly 1,000 halts a day for every 8,000 GPUs ⚠️. Meta says the first phase trained its Muse models ⚠️.

How far apart?

Distances between linked buildings, on a log scale. Fairwater figure is a straight-line approximation.

Light in fiber travels about 1 km in 5 µs, so 100 km adds at least 0.5 ms each way; Wisconsin to Atlanta adds about 5 ms.

Keeping the job running

Halts per day for 8,000 GPUs, before and after, as reported. The "after" bar is computed from the reported 99% reduction.

6. Power, two ways

Ohio. Prometheus follows Colossus in generating its own power. Meta worked with Williams on a $1.6 billion on-site natural gas generation system and pipeline infrastructure that runs behind the meter, and local officials said Meta would not be drawing from the local grid for it.

Louisiana. Hyperion follows Rainier in relying on a utility. In August 2025 the Louisiana Public Service Commission voted 4–1 to approve Entergy Louisiana's plan for three gas plants of about 754 MW each, roughly 2.26 GW, plus transmission. In March 2026 Entergy said Meta would fund seven more, bringing the total to ten; one report puts the combined capacity at 7.7 GW ⚠️ and cost estimates range from about $11 billion to $12.9 billion ⚠️. Regulators held hearings on the expansion in October 2026.

Gas plants for Hyperion

Approved and planned Entergy capacity in gigawatts.

7. The money

Hyperion is financed like Abilene, but with a hyperscaler as tenant. In October 2025 Meta formed a joint venture with funds managed by Blue Owl Capital: Blue Owl holds 80% and Meta 20%. Morgan Stanley arranged about $27.3 billion of bonds, rated A+ by S&P, repaid from Meta's rent. Meta leases the finished campus under an initial four-year operating lease with options to extend, and gives a capped residual value guarantee covering the first 16 years: if it leaves and the campus is worth less than a threshold, Meta pays the difference up to a cap. The structure keeps most of the cost off Meta's balance sheet.

8. Community and risk

Richland Parish is rural and relatively poor, and Hyperion is the largest private project in its history. The debate is over who carries the risk of the gas plants. Consumer advocates point out that the plants are designed to run for about 30 years while Meta's initial lease is four, and worry that ratepayers could be left paying for stranded plants if Meta leaves. Entergy and Meta say Meta pays for the plants under its agreement. The October 2026 hearings on the seven extra plants are where that argument is being tested.

⚖️ The four-year questionThe lease's short initial term is what makes it an operating lease for accounting. The residual value guarantee and renewal options protect bondholders, but they are not the same as a 30-year commitment to the plants. Who would pay if AI demand dropped is the unresolved question at Hyperion.

VerdictMeta shows where the industry is heading: no single bet, but every bet at once. Prometheus proves a frontier cluster can be stitched together from mismatched buildings if the software is good enough to keep it running. Hyperion proves investors will fund a 5 GW campus for a tenant with a four-year lease. Both depend on gas, and Hyperion's gas plants will outlive the lease. Next, Google's TPU fleet shows the company that built its own chips a decade before anyone else.

10. Reading the numbers

~1 GW and ~1 million GPU target; GB200/GB300 NVL72, Vera Rubin next; four building types; 2 km to 100+ km spans; 99% fewer interruptions ⚠️; Muse models ⚠️; Hyperion 5 GW and >$50B.
Regulators and utilities
Three ~754 MW Entergy plants approved 4–1 (Aug 2025); seven more announced (Mar 2026); 7.7 GW total and $11–12.9B cost are press figures ⚠️.
Financing
80/20 JV with Blue Owl; ~$27.3B A+ bonds; initial four-year lease with extension options; residual value guarantee for the first 16 years. Bloomberg described a 20-year lease, which likely includes extensions ⚠️.
